The Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo. Signed on February 2, 1848, in the small village of Guadalupe Hidalgo outside Mexico City. It ended the Mexican-American War and reshaped North America fundamentally. Mexico ceded roughly half its territory to the United States in exchange for fifteen million dollars. The U.S. extended its borders to the Pacific Ocean and became a continental power. For Mexico, it was a national catastrophe.

The Mexican-American War was fought from 1846 to 1848. American forces invaded Mexico, occupying Mexico City. Mexico, militarily defeated and politically fractured, was forced to negotiate, and the U.S. imposed harsh terms.

The territorial transfer was massive. Mexico ceded approximately five hundred twenty-five thousand square miles—California, Nevada, Utah, most of Arizona and New Mexico. That was roughly fifty-five percent of its territory. The Rio Grande became the boundary between Texas and Mexico, and that border, defined in this treaty, remains largely unchanged today. The United States acquired vast gold deposits, leading to the California Gold Rush just a year later in 1849. The U.S. also gained strategic Pacific coast territory.

The payment was paltry. Fifteen million dollars was offered as compensation for such vast lands. But the U.S. also assumed three point two five million dollars in claims by American citizens against Mexico, further reducing the net payment. In modern dollars, fifteen million is roughly five hundred million, but even that undervalues what the U.S. received. The payment did not offset Mexico's loss. Mexico was financially crippled for decades.

Roughly eighty thousand Mexicans lived in the ceded territories. They were given a choice: relocate to Mexico or become U.S. citizens. Most remained. They became a subordinate ethnic minority in the newly American Southwest. Their property rights were often violated.

The Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo exemplified U.S. Manifest Destiny—territorial expansion across the continent, regardless of indigenous and Mexican claims. For the U.S., it represented the fulfilment of an ideology of westward expansion, justifying conquest in the name of civilisational progress. The acquisition of the Southwest and California, with their mineral wealth and strategic value, made the U.S. a transcontinental power and set the stage for twentieth-century dominance. For Mexico, it was catastrophic. The loss of half its territory, the humiliation of military defeat, and a legacy of grievance and asymmetry have haunted U.S.-Mexican relations ever since. The wealth extracted from those lands—gold, cattle, oil—flowed to the United States, not Mexico. Mexican resentment persisted for generations. The treaty became a touchstone of nationalist feeling and a reminder of American imperialism. The treaty also precipitated the displacement and marginalisation of Native Americans in the West. The U.S. subsequently seized tribal lands as settlers moved westward. Today, the border defined by Guadalupe Hidalgo remains the front line of U.S.-Mexican relations, shaped entirely by this treaty's outcome.
